tiers.Robust (small scale): Reliably reproduced against this problem, but only in constructed or small-scale settings.
tiers.Strong existence proof: Shown convincingly at least once. Not yet reliable or general.
tiers.Early / partial: Positive but incomplete evidence, or the effect holds while the mechanism is unexplained.
tiers.Untested: Plausible mechanism proposed, but no direct empirical test yet.
tiers.Never demonstrated: Looked for and not found. The core claim has no instance despite attention.
tiers.Contested: Whether this addresses the problem is disputed, or the evidence cuts against it.
tiers.(blank): Not applicable. No meaningful relationship between this agenda and this problem.

familiarity_scale.1: General awareness but not active knowledge
familiarity_scale.2: Moderate familiarity, I follow work in this area
familiarity_scale.3: High familiarity, I have worked in or closely adjacent to this area
familiarity_scale.4: Expert, I work directly in this area

notes.Source of the scale: Taken from the supplied maturity assessment table, which uses Robust (small scale), Strong existence proof, Untested, Never demonstrated and Contested position. One tier was added: Early / partial, which absorbs the reference table's 'Strong, unexplained'. Untested and Never demonstrated are kept apart on purpose: no evidence and negative evidence are different findings.
notes.Two vocabularies: The same six tier words are used in two places. On the Agenda x Problem grid a tier rates evidence that an area addresses one specific problem. On the Agendas sheet the 'Overall maturity' column rates the research line as a technique in general. They can differ on purpose: a technique can be mature in general yet unproven against a particular problem.
notes.What a rating means: How mature the evidence is that this agenda addresses this specific problem. It is not a rating of the agenda's importance, nor of the research area's overall quality. The same agenda can be Robust against one problem and Contested against another.
notes.Contested is not a tie: Contested means evidence cuts against the agenda, or a real dispute is live in the literature. It is a stronger claim than Untested, not a weaker one. Where Contested is used, the Assumption cell on the Agendas sheet names the specific result that does the cutting.
notes.Familiarity (0-4): 0 = never heard of it. 1 = have read about it. 2 = have worked adjacent to it. 3 = have done research in it. 4 = expert, this is my area. Example entry: 2.
notes.Your input / notes: Open column. Disagree with a rating, add a missing agenda, or flag evidence we should look at. Example entry: 'DS1 x P7 Contested is an overcorrection, one paper is not a refutation.'

problems.name: Alignment measurement and observability
problems.short_def: No reliable way to confirm from the outside that a system is aligned. An aligned system and a deceptive one behave the same until they do not.

problems.name: Inner alignment and goal misgeneralization
problems.short_def: The model learns an internal objective that fit the training target but is not the target.

problems.name: Capability and alignment decoupling (sharp left turn)
problems.short_def: Capabilities generalize further than trained-in alignment, so good training behavior need not survive a capability jump.

problems.name: Deceptive alignment and scheming
problems.short_def: A model behaves aligned during training to protect a different objective.

problems.name: Outer alignment and specification
problems.short_def: Writing an objective that captures what we want without exploitable proxies.

problems.name: Scalable oversight
problems.short_def: We cannot directly supervise systems more capable than us. Using AI to help supervise AI risks recreating the problem one level up.

problems.name: Corrigibility and control
problems.short_def: Get systems to accept correction and shutdown, and stay safe even if misaligned. Has a ceiling once capability exceeds the control regime.

problems.name: Interpretability scaling
problems.short_def: Whether tools that read internal cognition scale to frontier systems or plateau.

problems.name: Evaluation validity and gaming
problems.short_def: Tests may not measure the intended property, and a model that knows it is being tested can pass without being safe.

problems.name: Competitiveness and the alignment tax
problems.short_def: Safe methods may be too slow or too weak to be adopted under competitive pressure.

problems.name: Threat model and takeoff uncertainty
problems.short_def: Which research looks useful depends on which disaster you expect, and the field has not settled this.

problems.name: Research misallocation
problems.short_def: The field may work on tractable proxies rather than central bottlenecks, because proxies give feedback and the central problems do not.

areas.name: Empirical Alignment
areas.definition: Training models using RLHF, fine-tuning, and feedback signals to align with human preferences; audits for capability spillovers in training pipelines.

areas.name: Interpretability
areas.definition: Mechanistic and developmental approaches to auditing AI internals, detecting deception or misalignment; moderation protocols to redact circuit insights that could improve capabilities.

areas.name: Adversarial Robustness
areas.definition: Methods for hardening models against adversarial attacks and distributional shifts; redaction guidelines to prevent robustness tools from enhancing general performance evaluations.

areas.name: Deployment Safety
areas.definition: Operational protocols for safe AI rollout including corrigibility and shutdown mechanisms; moderated to exclude techniques reusable for unrestricted agent scaling.

areas.name: Scalable Oversight
areas.definition: Methods such as debate, amplification, and recursive oversight for supervising superhuman AI; contributions may be redacted when they could support capability amplification.

areas.name: Alignment Foundations
areas.definition: Theoretical work on alignment problems, threat modeling, agent foundations, and formal verification; strict moderation to avoid foundational insights accelerating power-seeking behaviors.

areas.name: Capabilities Evaluation
areas.definition: Scientific study of AI capabilities including evaluations of emergence and scaling behavior; benchmarks may be redacted in controlled sharing to avoid informing capability roadmaps.

areas.name: Safety Assurance
areas.definition: Transparency tools, auditing, red teaming, and chain-of-thought monitoring for empirical safety verification; emphasizes aggregate findings rather than exploitable methodologies.

areas.name: Security Hardening
areas.definition: Defenses against misuse, jailbreaks, and security vulnerabilities; may require classification where prevention techniques could serve as evasion tools for capabilities research.

areas.name: Socio-Technical Safety
areas.definition: Integration of social, institutional, and technical factors for holistic alignment including governance interfaces; redaction policies may apply to dual-use socio-technical models.

areas.name: Safety Metaresearch
areas.definition: Research on the impact of safety work itself, including CSP frameworks for forecasting spillovers; prioritized for moderation to support safety without generating capability roadmaps.

areas.name: Technical AI Governance
areas.definition: Technical tools for governance including verification and policy enforcement mechanisms; contribution protocols prevent formal methods from enabling unchecked scaling.

agendas.mechanism: Human comparisons train a reward model; the policy is optimized against it.
agendas.assumption: Raters can judge the outputs that matter, and the reward model does not come apart under optimization. Wen et al. 2024 find RLHF can train models to mislead human evaluators rather than to be correct.
agendas.key_work: Christiano et al. 2017; Casper et al. 2023 (critique); Wen et al. 2024 (arXiv 2409.12822)

agendas.mechanism: The model critiques and revises its own outputs against a written spec; preference labels come from the model rather than humans.
agendas.assumption: The critic is honest about outputs it also produced, and the written spec generalizes past its examples.
agendas.key_work: Bai et al. 2022 (arXiv 2212.08073)

agendas.mechanism: Train the model to reason explicitly over a safety specification before answering.
agendas.assumption: Reasoning over the spec transfers to cases the spec did not anticipate, and the stated reasoning drives the output.
agendas.key_work: Guan et al. 2024 (OpenAI)

agendas.mechanism: Train against scheming-relevant behavior in constructed environments using spec reasoning.
agendas.assumption: Reduced observed scheming means reduced scheming rather than better concealment. MacDiarmid et al. 2025 found RLHF safety training produced aligned chat behavior while misalignment persisted on agentic tasks, which is this assumption failing.
agendas.key_work: Schoen et al. 2025 (OpenAI / Apollo); MacDiarmid et al. 2025 (arXiv 2511.18397)

agendas.agenda: Process supervision and robust reward modeling
agendas.mechanism: Supervise reasoning steps rather than final outcomes only.
agendas.assumption: The legible steps carry the computation that actually produces the answer.
agendas.key_work: Lightman et al. 2023 (arXiv 2305.20050)

agendas.mechanism: Deliberately induce the failure mode, then test whether current methods detect or remove it.
agendas.assumption: Induced failures resemble emergent ones. Sleeper agents implanted a backdoor and Hubinger et al. explicitly declined to claim the threat model is likely. MacDiarmid et al. 2025 closed part of that gap by getting misalignment to arise from reward hacking in real production RL rather than by implanting it. An open-source replication (Mar 2026) reproduced the reward hacking but got inconsistent emergent misalignment, so the effect is not yet established outside Anthropic's stack.
agendas.key_work: Hubinger et al. 2024 (arXiv 2401.05566); MacDiarmid et al. 2025 (arXiv 2511.18397); Betley et al. 2025

agendas.mechanism: Learn a sparse overcomplete basis that decomposes activations into candidate features.
agendas.assumption: The computation is sparse and linearly represented in the recovered basis. In the one blind test available, an SAE result was matched by a plain semantic-search baseline that does not touch the model at all.
agendas.key_work: Bricken et al. 2023; Templeton et al. 2024; Huben et al. 2024; Karvonen et al. 2025 (SAEBench, arXiv 2503.09532)

agendas.mechanism: Reverse engineer the specific computation responsible for a behavior.
agendas.assumption: Behavior decomposes into human-legible circuits, and the decomposition survives scale.
agendas.key_work: Marks et al. 2025 (sparse feature circuits, ICLR)

agendas.mechanism: Locate concept directions in activation space, then read or intervene on them.
agendas.assumption: Safety-relevant concepts have stable, linearly accessible directions.
agendas.key_work: Zou et al. 2023 (arXiv 2310.01405)

agendas.mechanism: Train a classifier on internals to read a property the model does not state.
agendas.assumption: The property is decodable from internals, and the probe learns that property rather than a correlate.
agendas.key_work: Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025 (deception probes, ICML); Clymer et al. 2024 (Poser, arXiv 2405.05466)

agendas.mechanism: Track structure formation across training rather than inspecting the final model.
agendas.assumption: Phase changes during training are visible and safety-relevant.
agendas.key_work: No landmark result identified

agendas.mechanism: A red team trains a model with a known hidden objective behind an information barrier; blue teams investigate and are graded on whether they find it.
agendas.assumption: Auditors have training-data access, and the objective leaves a findable trace in that data. In Marks et al. all three winning teams succeeded by locating the synthetic documents in the training corpus; the fourth team, given only API access and no data, failed. The authors also state the objective was explicitly described in training data, which may make the game unrealistically easy.
agendas.key_work: Marks et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.10965); Bricken et al. 2025 (auditing agents)

agendas.mechanism: Test whether stated reasoning causally drives the answer.
agendas.assumption: Faithfulness is measurable, and current architectures externalize the reasoning they need.
agendas.key_work: Turpin et al. 2023; Arcuschin et al. 2025; Lanham et al. 2023

agendas.mechanism: Generate attacks, train against them, iterate.
agendas.assumption: The attack distribution you can generate covers the one you will face. In the sleeper-agents setting adversarial training taught models to recognize their triggers and hide the behavior rather than removing it.
agendas.key_work: Hubinger et al. 2024 (arXiv 2401.05566)

agendas.mechanism: Study and improve behavior under distribution shift.
agendas.assumption: Benchmark shifts resemble deployment shifts.
agendas.key_work: Broad literature, no single landmark

agendas.mechanism: Construct environments where capability and goal generalize differently; test out of distribution with capability retained.
agendas.assumption: Constructed environments generalize to real training.
agendas.key_work: Langosco et al. 2022; Shah et al. 2022 (arXiv 2210.01790)

agendas.mechanism: Assume the model may be scheming; use a trusted weaker model to monitor, edit, defer, or resample its outputs, and bound what it can do.
agendas.assumption: A trusted weaker model is available AND the untrusted model cannot compromise the monitor. Terekhov et al. show the second half fails: an untrusted model that knows the protocol (which control's own threat model grants it) can embed prompt injections that collapse every monitor-based protocol to the safety of upfront auditing. GPT-4.1 scored all 375 backdoored samples as fully benign. Defer-to-Resample backfired, amplifying the injection into a best-of-n attack. Emmons et al. report injections failing to subvert monitors in their setting, so this is live dispute rather than settled refutation.
agendas.key_work: Greenblatt et al. 2024 (arXiv 2312.06942, ICML); Bhatt et al. 2025 (Ctrl-Z, arXiv 2504.10374); Terekhov et al. 2025 (arXiv 2510.09462); Emmons et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.05246)

agendas.mechanism: Design objectives or training such that the system accepts correction and shutdown.
agendas.assumption: Corrigibility is compatible with competent goal-directedness.
agendas.key_work: Soares et al. 2015; Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017 (off-switch game)

agendas.mechanism: Restrict affordances, permissions, and network access at the infrastructure layer.
agendas.assumption: The deployment surface is enumerable and the system stays inside the containable regime. Note this is the one place in the matrix with robust evidence, and it is the least AI-specific agenda here: it inherits its reliability from ordinary systems security, not from anything we understand about the model.
agendas.key_work: Standard security practice; CaMeL (Debenedetti et al. 2025, arXiv 2503.18813) for the injection-resistant design case

agendas.mechanism: Monitor communication between model instances for coordination.
agendas.assumption: Collusion is legible in the monitored channel rather than in a side channel.
agendas.key_work: No landmark result identified

agendas.mechanism: Two models argue; a weaker judge decides; truth is assumed easier to defend than falsehood.
agendas.assumption: Truth has an argumentative advantage, and the judge is not exploitable.
agendas.key_work: Irving et al. 2018 (arXiv 1805.00899); Khan et al. 2024; Brown-Cohen et al. 2023 (doubly-efficient debate)

agendas.agenda: Iterated amplification and recursive reward modeling
agendas.mechanism: Decompose a hard judgment into easier sub-judgments a human can check, recursively.
agendas.assumption: Judgment decomposes without losing the thing you cared about.
agendas.key_work: Christiano et al. 2018 (arXiv 1810.08575); Leike et al. 2018

agendas.mechanism: Fine-tune a strong model on a weak supervisor's labels and test whether it exceeds the supervisor.
agendas.assumption: Eliciting latent capability is the same problem as eliciting latent alignment. The effect is real but small: in the reward-model setting Burns et al. recover roughly 10 percent of the weak-to-strong performance gap, rarely above 20 percent, and they conclude naive weak supervision will be insufficient for superalignment. Later work finds weak training can degrade the strong model's reasoning.
agendas.key_work: Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv 2312.09390); Somerstep et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024

agendas.mechanism: Place a model between a non-expert and an expert; test whether non-expert plus model reaches expert quality.
agendas.assumption: Today's expertise gap proxies tomorrow's capability gap.
agendas.key_work: Bowman et al. 2022 (arXiv 2211.03540)

agendas.mechanism: Train for outputs a weaker verifier can check, trading performance for checkability.
agendas.assumption: Legibility to a weak verifier tracks correctness.
agendas.key_work: Kirchner et al. 2024 (arXiv 2407.13692)

agendas.mechanism: Study how real reviewers degrade under automation bias and throughput pressure, then design the process around it.
agendas.assumption: Process design holds against deployment volume and speed.
agendas.key_work: Engels et al. 2025 (scaling laws for scalable oversight, NeurIPS)

agendas.mechanism: Build formal models of embedded, self-modifying agents to say what alignment would even mean.
agendas.assumption: Formal agency models bind real trained systems.
agendas.key_work: Demski and Garrabrant 2019

agendas.mechanism: Predict when training produces an internal optimizer running its own objective.
agendas.assumption: Models implement search. Two claims must be kept apart. That transformers implement something like an internal optimization procedure during in-context learning has partial support (von Oswald et al.). That a trained model runs an internal search over its own objective distinct from the training objective, which is the safety-relevant claim and the one rated here, has no demonstrated instance.
agendas.key_work: Hubinger et al. 2019 (arXiv 1906.01820); von Oswald et al. 2023 (arXiv 2309.05858, partial and contested)

agendas.mechanism: Find a training scheme that reports what the model knows rather than what a human would say.
agendas.assumption: There is a fact of the matter about what the model knows, and it is elicitable.
agendas.key_work: Christiano, Xu, Cotra 2021 (ARC report)

agendas.mechanism: Prove that optimal policies for most objectives seek power under stated conditions.
agendas.assumption: The formal conditions apply to trained systems. Turner, who proved the original results, later argued publicly that they have been overinterpreted by the safety community.
agendas.key_work: Turner et al. 2019-2021 (arXiv 1912.01683); Turner's later retrospective posts

agendas.mechanism: Show that different systems converge on the same abstractions, so human concepts are targetable.
agendas.assumption: Natural abstractions exist and are shared across systems.
agendas.key_work: Wentworth, natural abstraction sequence

agendas.mechanism: Reward shapes contextual decision influences rather than installing a utility function.
agendas.assumption: None stated. It is a reframing, not a mechanism with a test attached, which is why it cannot be moved off Contested by evidence either way.
agendas.key_work: Pope and Turner 2022 (shard theory sequence)

agendas.agenda: Formal verification and guaranteed safe AI
agendas.mechanism: Specify a safety envelope formally and prove the system stays inside it.
agendas.assumption: The world model and the specification are adequate to the deployment environment.
agendas.key_work: Dalrymple et al. 2024 (Guaranteed Safe AI, arXiv 2405.06624)

agendas.agenda: Sharp left turn theory and refinements
agendas.mechanism: Capabilities generalize further than alignment across a phase change in capability.
agendas.assumption: None stated. The mechanism is asserted rather than specified, and Krakovna et al.'s refinement is an attempt to supply one.
agendas.key_work: Soares 2022; Krakovna et al. 2022 (refining the sharp left turn)

agendas.mechanism: Measure whether a model can perform a specified dangerous task under elicitation.
agendas.assumption: Elicitation is good enough that failure means inability rather than sandbagging.
agendas.key_work: Phuong et al. 2024 (arXiv 2403.13793)

agendas.mechanism: Extrapolate capability from compute and data.
agendas.assumption: The quantity you can extrapolate is the one you care about.
agendas.key_work: Kaplan et al. 2020; Schaeffer et al. 2023 (emergence as mirage)

agendas.mechanism: Test whether a model can acquire resources and copy itself.
agendas.assumption: The eval harness approximates a real adversarial setting.
agendas.key_work: METR autonomy evaluations

agendas.mechanism: Measure the length of task a model completes reliably, then track the doubling time.
agendas.assumption: Task length is the right axis, and the task suite stays representative.
agendas.key_work: METR 2025 (time horizons)

agendas.mechanism: Make dated public forecasts, then score them against outcomes.
agendas.assumption: The domain is forecastable enough that calibration transfers.
agendas.key_work: Kokotajlo, AI Futures Project; Kokotajlo's own forecast post-mortems

agendas.mechanism: A structured argument from claims to evidence that a system is safe to deploy.
agendas.assumption: The case's assumptions are independent enough that it does not fail all at once.
agendas.key_work: Clymer et al. 2024 (arXiv 2403.10462); Korbak et al. 2025 (control safety case sketch, arXiv 2501.17315); Balesni et al. 2024

agendas.mechanism: Humans and models search for inputs that produce failure.
agendas.assumption: Absence of found failures is informative about absence of failures.
agendas.key_work: Perez et al. 2022 (red teaming LMs with LMs)

agendas.mechanism: Read the reasoning trace for stated intent before acting on the output.
agendas.assumption: The model externalizes reasoning it needs, and training does not push it latent. Korbak et al., a 41-author position paper, argue this window is real but fragile: scaled RL and latent-reasoning architectures could close it, and Baker et al. show that optimizing against a CoT monitor teaches obfuscation.
agendas.key_work: Korbak et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.11473); Baker et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.11926); Emmons et al. 2025 (arXiv 2507.05246)

agendas.mechanism: Detect whether the model knows it is being tested, and whether it underperforms deliberately.
agendas.assumption: Evaluation-awareness is detectable from behavior or internals.
agendas.key_work: van der Weij, Hofstatter, Jaffe, Brown, Ward (sandbagging); Laine et al. 2024 (SAD, situational awareness dataset)

agendas.mechanism: Construct a conflict between the training objective and a goal the model holds, then see whether it games the conflict.
agendas.assumption: The constructed setup elicits the behavior real incentives would. The headline number is a compliance gap of roughly 14 percent in Claude 3 Opus, and whether that is real alignment faking or an artifact of a heavily scaffolded setup is the live interpretive dispute.
agendas.key_work: Greenblatt et al. 2024 (arXiv 2412.14093); Meinke et al. 2024 (in-context scheming, arXiv 2412.04984); Kutasov et al. 2025 (SHADE-Arena)

agendas.mechanism: Independent parties run evaluations under structured access.
agendas.assumption: Access is deep enough to be informative, and the auditor is not captured. The single controlled test of this is unflattering: in Marks et al.'s auditing game the only external team, given the API-only affordances a real third-party auditor typically gets, failed to find the hidden objective while all three teams with weights and training data succeeded.
agendas.key_work: Marks et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.10965), team 4 result

agendas.mechanism: Classifiers and training that hold refusals under adversarial user pressure.
agendas.assumption: The harm originates in the request rather than in the model's own objectives.
agendas.key_work: Sharma et al. 2025 (constitutional classifiers); Wallace et al. 2024 (instruction hierarchy, arXiv 2404.13208)

agendas.mechanism: Secure the weights against theft by outsiders and self-exfiltration by the model.
agendas.assumption: The threat surface is enumerable.
agendas.key_work: RAND security levels (Nevo et al. 2024)

agendas.mechanism: Remove a capability from the weights rather than refusing to use it.
agendas.assumption: Capabilities are localizable, and removal is not merely suppression. Repeated results find relearning or elicitation recovers supposedly unlearned capabilities.
agendas.key_work: Lynch et al. 2024 (eight methods to evaluate robust unlearning, arXiv 2402.16835)

agendas.mechanism: Study emergent dynamics between agents and between their principals.
agendas.assumption: Multi-agent effects are studyable below deployment scale.
agendas.key_work: Critch 2021 (multipolar failure)

agendas.mechanism: Harden the information environment and human epistemics against AI persuasion.
agendas.assumption: Defense scales with offense.
agendas.key_work: Durmus et al. 2024 (measuring persuasiveness)

agendas.mechanism: Model slow, non-takeover loss of human agency through economic and institutional substitution.
agendas.assumption: The failure mode is real and distinguishable from ordinary automation.
agendas.key_work: Kulveit et al. 2025 (gradual disempowerment, arXiv 2501.16946)

agendas.mechanism: Enumerate problems and agendas, then look at what nobody is working on. This project sits here.
agendas.assumption: The problem taxonomy is right, or at least not systematically blind.
agendas.key_work: Larsen 2022; Hobbhahn et al. 2023 (shallow review of live agendas)

agendas.mechanism: Ask whether a piece of safety work advances capability more than it advances safety.
agendas.assumption: Safety and capability contributions are separable enough to compare.
agendas.key_work: Critch, differential progress posts

agendas.mechanism: Articulate what makes a research question good when feedback is sparse.
agendas.assumption: Research taste is transmissible rather than tacit.
agendas.key_work: Karnofsky 2022; Shimi et al. 2021-2022 (epistemic strategies)

agendas.mechanism: Survey agendas and state explicit bets on which look healthiest.
agendas.assumption: Reviewers can judge areas outside their own. This is what the familiarity column is for.
agendas.key_work: Hobbhahn et al. 2023; Larsen 2022

agendas.mechanism: Pre-commit to capability thresholds and required mitigations before training.
agendas.assumption: The commitments bind under competitive pressure. Untested precisely because no threshold has yet been hit at a point where honouring it would cost a lab a release.
agendas.key_work: Anthropic RSP; OpenAI Preparedness Framework; Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework

agendas.mechanism: Use the compute supply chain as an enforceable chokepoint.
agendas.assumption: Compute stays concentrated, and verification is technically feasible.
agendas.key_work: Sastry et al. 2024 (computing power and governance)

agendas.mechanism: Standardized disclosure and structured access so safety claims can be checked.
agendas.assumption: Disclosure is honest and useful without leaking capability.
agendas.key_work: Bucknall and Trager 2023 (structured access)

priorities.intro: Priority is not importance. Every problem in this map matters. This section ranks by the gap between how load-bearing a problem is and how much solid evidence exists against it, i.e. the problems the rest of the map leans on hardest while resting on the least-finished work. Leverage comes from the dependency structure in the Problems document; evidence comes straight from the verified Agenda x Problem matrix. For each problem the listed research areas are the ones whose agendas actually reach it, so a promising direction is never confused with a proven one.

tier_descriptions.Tier 1 Critical: High leverage in the dependency graph AND best evidence is weak, untested, or contested. The map leans on these and the floor is not there.
tier_descriptions.Tier 2 High: Very high leverage with only partial evidence, or thin coverage on a problem that feeds others.
tier_descriptions.Tier 3 Notable: A real gap worth naming, but less load-bearing or with at least one existence proof to build on.

items.why_unsolved:
The hub of the whole map.
Role: the Problems document is explicit that nearly everything else matters because it makes verification of P1 impossible or unreliable.
Why hard: an aligned system and a deceptive one behave identically until they do not.
Consequence: without progress here, every downstream safety case inherits an unverified premise.

items.why_unsolved:
Conditions much of the near-term agenda.
Role: most near-term safety work assumes we can oversee systems more capable than us.
Why hard: the document flags its circularity, using AI to supervise AI risks recreating the problem one level up.
Dependency: rests on P1 and on honesty/ELK, so it inherits P1's weakness on top of its own.

Best evidence: 2 existence proofs (weak-to-strong, and a debate result).
Caveat: weak-to-strong recovers only ~10-20% of the supervisor-student gap, and its own authors call naive weak supervision insufficient.
Floor: 7 of 13 cells are only Early/partial.

items.why_unsolved:
The failure mode that makes P1 hard, not a separate track.
Role: a scheming model is exactly the case measurement cannot catch.
Dependency: depends on P1, P2 and situational awareness.
Why Tier 2 not 1: better studied than most problems here, but the interpretive picture is contested.

Caveat: also 3 Contested cells.
Disputed headline: Claude 3 Opus complied with harmful monitored (free-tier) queries 14% of the time versus almost never when unmonitored; interpretation is contested (Sheshadri et al. 2025 found a gap above 1% in only 5 of 25 models).

items.problem_name: P3  Capability and alignment decoupling (sharp left turn)
items.why_unsolved:
The training-level worry behind why good behavior need not survive a capability jump.
Role: load-bearing for the whole threat model.
Dependency: depends on P2 and on takeoff assumptions (P11).
Gap: second-thinnest in coverage of all twelve problems.

priorities.reading_note: Two of the top four (P1, P6) are the oversight-and-measurement problems the rest of the map depends on, and none of the six has a single Robust cell. The one place in the whole matrix with robust evidence, sandboxing against P7, is the least AI-specific agenda in it and inherits its reliability from ordinary systems security. The pattern is consistent: the field's most load-bearing problems rest on its least-finished work. Agenda names and the detail behind every tier are on the Agendas sheet; cell-by-cell ratings and source checks are on Agenda x Problem.
